prompt: Four cards are placed in this order: 2, 0, 1, 7. Which order **cannot** be obtained if only two cards are swapped?

solutions.title: Check each order
solutions.body:
Compare each order with 2017 and see which cards moved.
- **(A) 2710:** the 0 and the 7 changed places → one swap.
- **(B) 0127:** the 2, the 0 and the 1 all moved → that needs more than one swap.
- **(C) 1027:** the 2 and the 1 changed places → one swap.
- **(D) 0217:** the 2 and the 0 changed places → one swap.
- **(E) 2071:** the 1 and the 7 changed places → one swap.

**Answer: (B) 0127**

solutions.title: Count the cards that moved
solutions.body:
A single swap moves **exactly two** cards; the other two stay where they were.

In 0127, only the 7 is still in its place (the last spot). Three cards moved, so one swap is not enough. Every other choice keeps exactly two cards in place.

**Answer: (B) 0127**

prompt: A fly has 6 legs, a spider 8. Therefore 3 flies and 2 spiders together have the same number of legs as 9 chickens and …

solutions.title: Count all the legs
solutions.body:
Flies: $3 \times 6 = 18$ legs. Spiders: $2 \times 8 = 16$ legs. Together: $18 + 16 = 34$ legs.

Chickens: $9 \times 2 = 18$ legs. Legs left for cats: $34 - 18 = 16$. Each cat has 4 legs: $16 \div 4 = 4$ cats.

**Answer: (C) 4 cats**

solutions.title: Match the groups
solutions.body:
The 3 flies have $18$ legs, exactly as many as the 9 chickens ($9 \times 2 = 18$). So the chickens "cancel" the flies.

That leaves the 2 spiders with $16$ legs, which must equal the cats. $16 = 4 \times 4$, so 4 cats.

**Answer: (C) 4 cats**

prompt: Anna has four identical building blocks that each look like this (a straight row of 3 squares). Which shape can she **not** form with them?

solutions.title: Try the corner squares
solutions.body:
Each shape has $4 \times 3 = 12$ squares, so counting alone doesn't help. Look at squares that have only one way to be covered.

In **(E)** the bottom-left square has nothing above it, so its block must lie flat: it covers the first three bottom squares. The last bottom square then needs a standing block, which uses the squares above it in the middle row and top row. Now the left square of the middle row is stuck: the squares to its right and below it are used, and there is nothing to its left or above it that is free. It cannot be covered.

The other four shapes can all be built (for example, (C) uses one standing block on the right of the left part and three lying blocks).

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Build the others
solutions.body:
Show that (A)–(D) work, so (E) must be the one that fails.
- **(A)** The square ring: put one block along each side, each sticking out past a corner like a pinwheel.
- **(B)** The $3 \times 4$ rectangle: four blocks side by side.
- **(C)** One block standing in the 4th column and three blocks lying flat.
- **(D)** Two standing blocks (one at each bump) and two lying blocks in the bottom row.

In (E) the middle row is shifted so its left square is left alone after the bottom row is filled, and no block can reach it.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: Kevin knows that $1111 \times 1111 = 1234321$. Which result does he get for $1111 \times 2222$?

solutions.title: Check the last digit and the size
solutions.body:
$1 \times 2$ ends in 2, so the answer ends in 2: that leaves (B), (C) and (D).

The answer is about $1000 \times 2000 = 2\,000\,000$ but more than $1111 \times 2000 = 2\,222\,000$. Only (D) 2468642 is bigger than 2222000 among (B), (C), (D).

**Answer: (D) 2468642**

prompt: The 10 islands are connected by 12 bridges (see diagram). All bridges are open for traffic. What is the minimum number of bridges that need to be closed off, so that traffic between A and B comes to a halt?

solutions.title: Find two separate routes
solutions.body:
There is a route along the top: A → top island → top-right island → right island → B.

There is a route along the bottom: A → island below A → bottom-left island → bottom-middle island → B.

These two routes share no bridge, so closing just 1 bridge leaves the other route open. We need at least 2.

Closing 2 is enough: close the bridge from A down to the island below it, and the bridge from the top-right island down to the right island. Now every path from A ends in a dead end.

**Answer: (B) 2**

solutions.title: Look at the bottlenecks
solutions.body:
Everything from A to B must cross either the left side or the top-right side.
- On the left, A is joined to the lower islands only by **one** bridge (A to the island below it).
- The top islands reach B only through the **one** bridge from the top-right island to the right island.

Close those two bridges and A is cut off from B. One bridge is not enough, because there are two routes that don't share any bridge.

**Answer: (B) 2**

prompt: Jane, Kate and Lynn go for a walk. Jane walks at the very front, Kate in the middle and Lynn at the very back. Jane weighs 500 kg more than Kate and Kate weighs 1000 kg less than Lynn. Which of the following pictures shows Jane, Kate and Lynn in the right order? (In the picture, the label (D) is at the end of the first row; its picture is the first one in the second row.)

solutions.title: Sort by weight
solutions.body:
Compare everyone to Kate:
- Jane = Kate + 500 kg
- Lynn = Kate + 1000 kg

So Kate is the lightest (smallest), Jane is in the middle, and Lynn is the heaviest (biggest).

The rhinos face left, so the front is on the left. From left to right we need: medium (Jane), small (Kate), big (Lynn). That is picture (A).

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Pick numbers
solutions.body:
Say Kate weighs 1000 kg. Then Jane weighs 1500 kg and Lynn weighs 2000 kg.

Walking left (the way the rhinos look): front Jane 1500, middle Kate 1000, back Lynn 2000. So the order is medium – small – big. Only (A) shows that.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: Max colours in the squares of the grid, so that one third of all squares are blue and one half of all squares are yellow. The rest he colours red. How many squares does he have to colour red?

solutions.title: Count the squares
solutions.body:
The grid has 3 rows of 6 squares: $3 \times 6 = 18$ squares.

Blue: $\frac{1}{3}$ of 18 = 6. Yellow: $\frac{1}{2}$ of 18 = 9. Red: $18 - 6 - 9 = 3$.

**Answer: (C) 3**

solutions.title: Add the fractions
solutions.body:
Blue and yellow together are $\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{6} + \frac{3}{6} = \frac{5}{6}$. So red is $\frac{1}{6}$ of the grid.

$\frac{1}{6}$ of 18 squares is 3.

**Answer: (C) 3**

prompt: Bob folds a piece of paper, then punches a hole into the paper and unfolds it again. The unfolded paper then looks like this. Along which dotted line has Bob folded the paper beforehand?

solutions.title: Count the layers
solutions.body:
One punch made 4 holes, so the paper had 4 layers. (E) has only 2 fold lines, which gives just 3 layers. (A) and (C) would give 4 holes in a square pattern, and the vertical lines of (B) would put the holes in a horizontal row.

The holes lie on a slanted line from top left to bottom right, equally spaced. Folding back and forth (like a fan) along the **three slanted lines** of (D) stacks 4 strips on top of each other. A single punch goes through all 4 strips, and the holes appear one in each strip, along a line that crosses the folds at a right angle — exactly the picture.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Mirror the holes
solutions.body:
When you unfold, every hole is mirrored across the fold line. So neighbouring holes must be mirror images across a fold.

The line joining the holes goes from top left to bottom right. Mirror lines between them must cross this line at a right angle, i.e. go from bottom left to top right, and lie halfway between neighbouring holes. With 4 holes we need 3 such lines. That is choice (D).

(B) and (E) have vertical lines, which would put the holes in a horizontal row; (A) and (C) would make 4 holes in a square pattern.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: A rectangle is twice as long as it is wide. Which fraction of the rectangle is coloured grey?

solutions.title: Use easy numbers
solutions.body:
Make the rectangle 4 long and 2 wide, so its area is 8. The diagonals cross in the middle, at height 1.
- The grey triangle on the left has the left side (2) as base and reaches to the middle (2 across): area $\frac{2 \times 2}{2} = 2$.
- The grey triangle at the bottom right has base 2 (from the middle to the right corner) and height 1: area $\frac{2 \times 1}{2} = 1$.

Grey: $2 + 1 = 3$ out of 8.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{3}{8}$**

solutions.title: Cut into pieces
solutions.body:
The two diagonals cut the rectangle into 4 triangles. The left and right triangles are each $\frac{1}{4}$ of the rectangle (same for top and bottom).

The left grey triangle is $\frac{1}{4}$.

The vertical line cuts the bottom triangle into two equal halves, so the grey bottom-right piece is $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{8}$.

Total: $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{2}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{3}{8}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{3}{8}$**

prompt: Only four players score goals in a handball game. Each one scored a different number of goals. Michael scored the fewest goals. If the other players together scored 20 goals in total, what is the maximum number of goals Michael could have scored?

solutions.title: Try the choices from the top
solutions.body:
The other three each scored more than Michael, and all different.
- Michael 6: the others score at least $7 + 8 + 9 = 24 > 20$. No.
- Michael 5: at least $6 + 7 + 8 = 21 > 20$. No.
- Michael 4: for example $5 + 6 + 9 = 20$. Yes!

**Answer: (C) 4**

solutions.title: Smallest possible total
solutions.body:
If Michael scored $m$ goals, the other three scored at least $m+1$, $m+2$ and $m+3$, which add up to $3m + 6$.

This must be at most 20: $3m + 6 \le 20$, so $3m \le 14$ and $m \le 4$.

$m = 4$ works with $5, 6, 9$ (or $5, 7, 8$).

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: A furniture shop sells 3-seater, 2-seater and 1-seater sofas that each have an equally wide armrest on the left and on the right hand side. Each seat is equally wide (see picture). Together with the armrests the 3-seater sofa is 220 cm and the 2-seater sofa 160 cm wide. How wide is the 1-seater sofa?

solutions.title: Take away one seat
solutions.body:
The 3-seater and the 2-seater have the same two armrests; the only difference is one seat. So one seat is $220 - 160 = 60$ cm wide.

The 1-seater has one seat less than the 2-seater: $160 - 60 = 100$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 100 cm**

solutions.title: Find the armrests
solutions.body:
One seat is $220 - 160 = 60$ cm (the difference between the sofas).

The 2-seater: two seats are $120$ cm, so the two armrests together are $160 - 120 = 40$ cm.

1-seater: $60 + 40 = 100$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 100 cm**

prompt: Tom strings together the numbers from 1 to 20 and obtains the 31-digit number 1234567891011121314151617181920. Then he deletes 24 digits of the number, so that the remaining number is as big as possible. Which number does he obtain?

solutions.title: Choose digits greedily
solutions.body:
He keeps $31 - 24 = 7$ digits. To make the number big, each digit (from the left) should be as big as possible.
- **1st digit:** there is only one 9 early on (in "…789"), so start with **9**. Everything before it is deleted.
- After the 9 comes 1011121314151617181920. We still need 6 digits, so the 2nd digit must come from far enough left that 5 digits remain after it. The biggest choice is the **7** of 17 (after it: 181920, which is 6 digits).
- 3rd digit: from 181920 we need 5 digits; the best start is **8** (after it 1920).
- The last 4 digits must be 1920.

Result: **9781920**.

**Answer: (C) 9781920**

solutions.title: Check the choices
solutions.body:
All choices start with 9. Look at the 2nd digit: the biggest 2nd digit among the choices is 9 in (D) 9912345, but there is only one 9 before "19", and after the 9 of 19 only "20" is left — too short. So (D) is impossible.

Next biggest 2nd digit is 8 in (E) 9818192 — but after the 8 of 18 only "1920" remains, 4 digits, and (E) needs 5 more. Impossible.

Then 7 in (C) 9781920: 9, then 7 of 17, then 8 of 18, then 1, 9, 2, 0. That works, and it beats (A) and (B).

**Answer: (C) 9781920**

prompt: There is a number written on every face of a special die. The sum of the numbers on opposite faces is always the same. Five of the six numbers are 5, 6, 9, 11 and 14. Which number is on the sixth face?

solutions.title: Find two pairs
solutions.body:
Two of the opposite pairs are among the five numbers. Look for two pairs with the same sum:

$6 + 14 = 20$ and $9 + 11 = 20$. 

So every pair adds to 20, and 5 is with the missing number: $20 - 5 = 15$.

**Answer: (E) 15**

solutions.title: Use the total
solutions.body:
There are 3 opposite pairs with the same sum, so the total of all six numbers must be 3 times that sum — it must divide by 3.

The five known numbers add up to $5 + 6 + 9 + 11 + 14 = 45$. Adding each choice: $45 + 4 = 49$, $45 + 7 = 52$, $45 + 8 = 53$, $45 + 13 = 58$, $45 + 15 = 60$. Only 60 divides by 3.

Check: each pair adds to $60 \div 3 = 20$: $5 + 15 = 6 + 14 = 9 + 11 = 20$. ✓

**Answer: (E) 15**

prompt: Paul goes on a 5-day hiking trek. He starts on Monday and finishes on Friday. Every day he covers 2 km more than the day before. In total he hikes 70 km. Which distance does he cover on Thursday?

solutions.title: Start from the middle day
solutions.body:
The distances go up evenly, so the middle day (Wednesday) is the average: $70 \div 5 = 14$ km.

Thursday is 2 km more: $14 + 2 = 16$ km.

(Check: $10 + 12 + 14 + 16 + 18 = 70$.)

**Answer: (E) 16 km**

solutions.title: Use Monday
solutions.body:
If Monday is $m$ km, the days are $m$, $m+2$, $m+4$, $m+6$, $m+8$. Together: $5m + 20 = 70$, so $5m = 50$ and $m = 10$.

Thursday: $m + 6 = 16$ km.

**Answer: (E) 16 km**

prompt: Boris wants to increase his pocket money. To achieve this, a fairy gives him three magic wands. He has to use every single one exactly once. Magic wand "+1" increases his money by 1 €, magic wand "−1" decreases it by 1 €, and magic wand "•2" doubles it. In which order (from left to right) does he have to use the magic wands to get the most money?

solutions.title: Try it with a number
solutions.body:
Say Boris starts with 10 €.
- (A) $10 \to 20 \to 21 \to 20$
- (B) $10 \to 11 \to 10 \to 20$
- (C) $10 \to 20 \to 19 \to 20$
- (D) $10 \to 11 \to 22 \to 21$
- (E) $10 \to 9 \to 10 \to 20$

Only (D) gives more: 21 €.

**Answer: (D) +1, •2, −1**

solutions.title: Double the good, not the bad
solutions.body:
Doubling also doubles whatever was added or taken away before it. So the best plan is: add 1 **before** doubling (the +1 becomes +2), and take 1 away **after** doubling (it stays just −1).

That is +1, then •2, then −1. Starting with $x$ €: $(x + 1) \times 2 - 1 = 2x + 1$, while every other order gives only $2x$.

**Answer: (D) +1, •2, −1**

prompt: Raphael has three squares. The first one has side length 2 cm. The second one has side length 4 cm and one of its corners is at the centre of the first square. The third square has side length 6 cm and one of its corners is at the centre of the second square. What is the total area of the figure shown?

solutions.title: Add, then subtract the overlaps
solutions.body:
Areas: $2 \times 2 = 4$, $4 \times 4 = 16$, $6 \times 6 = 36$. Together $56\text{ cm}^2$.

The second square starts at the centre of the first, so it covers one quarter of the first: $4 \div 4 = 1\text{ cm}^2$ counted twice. The third square covers one quarter of the second: $16 \div 4 = 4\text{ cm}^2$ counted twice.

Total: $56 - 1 - 4 = 51\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: (A) 51 cm²**

solutions.title: Add only the new parts
solutions.body:
Start with the big square: $36\text{ cm}^2$.

The middle square shows $\frac{3}{4}$ of itself outside the big one: $\frac{3}{4} \times 16 = 12\text{ cm}^2$.

The small square shows $\frac{3}{4}$ of itself outside the middle one: $\frac{3}{4} \times 4 = 3\text{ cm}^2$.

Total: $36 + 12 + 3 = 51\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: (A) 51 cm²**

prompt: A big cube is made up of 9 identical building blocks. Each building block looks like this: a row of 3 small cubes, grey, grey, white. Which big cube is possible?

solutions.title: Build (A)
solutions.body:
Lay all 9 blocks from left to right, in 3 layers of 3 rows.

Then each row of the front face is one block, so it reads grey-grey-white or white-grey-grey: in (A) the front rows are G G W, W G G, W G G. ✓ The top face also shows three whole blocks: W G G, W G G, G G W. ✓ The right face shows only the right ends of the 9 blocks, which can be white or grey in any pattern. ✓

So (A) can be built.

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Rule out the others
solutions.body:
A small cube has one colour, so a cube on an edge must look the same on both faces where you can see it.
- **(C)** and **(D):** the front-top row shows a white cube whose top is grey. Impossible.
- **(B):** the front-right column shows a white cube whose right side is grey. Impossible.
- **(E):** the centre of a face is grey if a block lies flat along that face (it is the block's middle). It can only be white if a block goes straight in through the **very middle cube** of the big cube. In (E) both the front centre and the right-side centre are white, so two blocks would need the same middle cube. Impossible.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 have to be written into the five fields of this diagram according to the following rules: if one number is below another number, it has to be greater; if one number is to the right of another, it has to be greater. How many ways are there to place the numbers?

solutions.title: Start with the corner
solutions.body:
The corner field has the other four fields to its right or below it, so it must hold the smallest number, **1**.

The remaining numbers 2, 3, 4, 5 are split: two go in the top row (to the right of 1) and two go in the column (below 1). In each pair the order is fixed (smaller first). So we just choose which 2 numbers go in the top row:

{2,3}, {2,4}, {2,5}, {3,4}, {3,5}, {4,5} → **6** ways.

**Answer: (D) 6**

solutions.title: List them
solutions.body:
1 is in the corner. Write the top row (right of 1) and the column (below 1):
1. top 2, 3 – column 4, 5
2. top 2, 4 – column 3, 5
3. top 2, 5 – column 3, 4
4. top 3, 4 – column 2, 5
5. top 3, 5 – column 2, 4
6. top 4, 5 – column 2, 3

That's 6 ways.

**Answer: (D) 6**

prompt: There are eight kangaroos in a row, as seen in the picture. Two kangaroos that are standing next to each other and looking into each other's eyes change places by hopping past each other. This is carried out until no more jumps are possible. How many times did a change of places occur?

solutions.title: Count the meetings
solutions.body:
From left to right the kangaroos face: right, right, right, left, right, right, left, left.

Right-facers move right and left-facers move left. Each jump lets one right-facer pass one left-facer, and every right-facer that starts left of a left-facer must pass it exactly once.
- The left-facer in place 4 has 3 right-facers to its left → 3 jumps.
- The left-facer in place 7 has 5 right-facers to its left → 5 jumps.
- The left-facer in place 8 has 5 right-facers to its left → 5 jumps.

Total: $3 + 5 + 5 = 13$.

**Answer: (D) 13**

solutions.title: Count from the right-facers
solutions.body:
Write R for right-facing and L for left-facing: R R R L R R L L.

At the end all L's are on the left and all R's on the right. Each jump swaps one neighbouring "R L" pair. For each R, count the L's to its right:
- The first three R's each have 3 L's to their right: $3 \times 3 = 9$.
- The R's in places 5 and 6 each have 2 L's to their right: $2 \times 2 = 4$.

Total: $9 + 4 = 13$ jumps.

**Answer: (D) 13**

prompt: A square floor is made up of triangular and square tiles in grey and white. What is the smallest number of grey tiles that have to be swapped with white tiles, so that the floor looks the same from all four given viewing directions?

solutions.title: Look for groups of four
solutions.body:
To look the same from all four sides, the floor must look the same after a quarter turn. Tiles come in groups of 4 that swap places under quarter turns; each group must be all grey or all white.

**Triangles:** the grey triangles at the top-left (left edge), top-right (top edge) and bottom-left (bottom edge) are 3 of one group of 4 — the 4th one, at the bottom of the right edge, is white. The 4th grey triangle (bottom edge, middle) is alone in its group. Move it to the missing spot: **1 triangle** swap.

**Squares:** three grey squares (top, left, bottom right) form 3 of a group of 4; the missing one is the white square on the right. The grey square just right of the centre is alone in its group. Move it to the missing spot: **1 square** swap.

**Answer: (C) one triangle, one square**

solutions.title: Count what each group needs
solutions.body:
There are 4 grey triangles and 4 grey squares, so after the swaps there will still be 4 of each — exactly one full group of 4 of each kind.

For each kind, one group already has 3 grey tiles and only one grey tile is somewhere else. Swapping that stray grey tile with the white gap fills the group. That is 1 swap for triangles and 1 swap for squares. Zero swaps can't work, because the floor doesn't look the same from all sides now.

**Answer: (C) one triangle, one square**

prompt: In a bag there are only red and green marbles. If one randomly takes out five marbles, there is at least one red one among them. If one randomly takes out six marbles, there is at least one green one among them. What is the maximum number of marbles in the bag?

solutions.title: Limit each colour
solutions.body:
- Any 5 marbles contain a red one, so there can't be 5 green marbles: **at most 4 green**.
- Any 6 marbles contain a green one, so there can't be 6 red marbles: **at most 5 red**.

So at most $4 + 5 = 9$ marbles. With 4 green and 5 red both rules hold: 5 marbles can't all be green, and 6 marbles can't all be red.

**Answer: (C) 9**

solutions.title: Test the choices
solutions.body:
Try 10 marbles: you would need at most 4 green and at most 5 red, but $4 + 5 = 9 < 10$. Too many — either there are 5 green (and you could take 5 greens) or 6 red (and you could take 6 reds). So 10 or 11 can't work.

9 works with 4 green and 5 red.

**Answer: (C) 9**

prompt: Each one of the 5 keys opens exactly one padlock. Every letter on a padlock stands for exactly one digit; same letters mean same digits. Which digits are on the key with the question mark?

solutions.title: Crack the code
solutions.body:
DAD has the same first and last letter. The only key with the same first and last digit is **414**, so D = 4 and A = 1.

ABD = 1?4: the key 124 fits, so B = 2.
AHD = 1?4: the key 184 fits, so H = 8.
HAB = 812 ✓ (that key is there).

The padlock without a key is BHD = **284**.

**Answer: (C) 284**

solutions.title: Use the last letter
solutions.body:
Three padlocks end in D (BHD, ABD, AHD) and DAD starts and ends with D. The digit 4 is at the end of 414, 124, 184 — so D = 4, and 414 must be DAD (A = 1).

HAB is the only padlock not ending in D, so it gets 812: H = 8, A = 1, B = 2.

BHD = 2, 8, 4 → 284.

**Answer: (C) 284**

prompt: Petra likes even numbers, Ina likes numbers that are divisible by 3, and Celina likes numbers that are divisible by 5. In a basket there are 8 balls, each with a number written on it. Each of the three girls went to the basket on her own and took all the balls with numbers she likes. Petra took 32 and 52, Ina took 24, 33 and 45, and Celina took 20, 25 and 35. In which order did they go to the basket?

solutions.title: Look for balls someone would have liked
solutions.body:
- 24 is even, but Petra didn't take it — Ina took it. So **Ina went before Petra**.
- 20 is even, but Celina took it. So **Celina went before Petra**.
- 45 is divisible by 5, but Ina took it. So **Ina went before Celina**.

Order: Ina, Celina, Petra.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Who went last?
solutions.body:
Petra took only 32 and 52. If she had been earlier, she would also have taken the even balls 24 and 20. So Petra went last.

Between Ina and Celina: 45 is liked by both (divisible by 3 and by 5). Ina got it, so Ina was first.

**Answer: (D) Ina, Celina, Petra**

prompt: The first kangaroo is repeatedly mirrored along the dotted lines. Two reflections have already been carried out. In which position is the kangaroo in the grey triangle?

solutions.title: Keep mirroring
solutions.body:
There are 6 triangles in the strip; the kangaroo is already in the first three. Mirror three more times.

A useful shortcut: two mirrorings in a row (across two lines that meet at a corner) are the same as a **turn**. Compare the 1st and 3rd triangles: the kangaroo has been turned so its head points down. The same thing happens from the 3rd to the 5th triangle, and from the 2nd to the 4th.

So the grey (6th) triangle holds the kangaroo of the 2nd triangle turned twice more. The 2nd kangaroo lies on its side with its head on the left; after the two turns its head points up to the right, its feet go down to the left and its tail hangs down. That is (E).

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Turn the 2nd kangaroo
solutions.body:
Two mirrorings across lines that meet at a corner of the triangles make a turn of one third of a full turn. Going from the 2nd triangle to the grey 6th triangle takes 4 mirrorings = two such turns in the same direction, which is the same as **one third of a turn the other way** (clockwise).

The kangaroo in the 2nd triangle has its head on the left, its tail sticking up and its feet to the right. Turn it a third of a turn clockwise: the head moves to the upper right, the tail points down and the feet go to the lower left. That is (E).

Check: the grey triangle is 5 mirrorings from the first one (an odd number), so it must be a mirror image of the first kangaroo. In (E) the kangaroo is upright but its legs and tail are swapped compared with the first one — a mirror image. ✓

**Answer: (E)**
